text: Rain ran off the shelter roof in a steady curtain, and I kept checking the road as if the bus might appear sooner if I watched hard enough. My interview folder was tucked beneath my shirt, but the pages had already curled at the edges. The phone in my hand showed one percent battery and a message from the clinic: Please arrive by nine or reschedule. My daughter’s appointment had taken six weeks to get. I called the clinic anyway, got the recorded menu, and pressed buttons with a thumb gone clumsy from cold. A woman beside me offered half her umbrella. I thanked her, then stepped to the curb when headlights rose through the rain. It was a delivery van. I lowered my hand, wiped my face with my sleeve, and looked down the empty street again.

At the bus stop, Malik counted the coins in his palm for the fourth time. The rain tapped his hood while water crept through one shoe. His toolbox sat between his feet; inside it was the only set of tools he owned, and a landlord had given him until noon to fix the leaking pipe upstairs. If he missed the morning shift, the repair shop would give his hours to someone else. He tried calling his supervisor, but the screen went black before the call connected. Across the street, the bus shelter clock showed 7:42. Malik stepped out to see around a parked truck, then retreated as a splash soaked his trousers. When the bus finally turned the corner, he lifted both arms, waving so urgently that a cyclist swerved around him. The driver braked, and Malik climbed aboard, still counting coins.

I had my mother’s ring in one fist and a bus pass in the other, though I couldn’t remember whether the pass had any rides left. The rain blurred the schedule posted inside the shelter. At the hospital, they were waiting for me to sign papers before they moved her into surgery, and each minute on the roadside seemed to drag its feet. I called my brother; the phone rang until it cut off. Then I called again, leaving a message that came out too fast to understand. My coat clung to my arms. A man asked whether I was all right, and I nodded without looking at him. When a bus approached, I leaned so far toward the road that the man caught my elbow. It wasn’t my route. I watched it carry its warm yellow windows away, then pressed the ring against my palm until its edges hurt.

Priya stood beneath the bus-stop sign with a paper bag held above her head. Inside it, her bakery’s first wedding cake leaned against a box of candles, and the rain had already softened one corner of the cardboard. The taxi app kept searching for a driver. She could see the hotel across town on the map, but the delivery van was in the garage for repairs, and her assistant had stopped answering. A bus was due in three minutes; Priya checked the clock, then the map, then the clock again. She asked a stranger if the route passed the hotel. It did, but the trip would take forty minutes. Her mouth tightened as she phoned the bride, rehearsing a cheerful explanation that would not come. When the bus arrived, she climbed aboard with both arms around the cake, shielding it from every jolt.

My backpack was soaking through, and the small plastic folder inside held every drawing I’d made for the scholarship review. I kept pressing its zipper closed, although water was already beading beneath the flap. The bus was late; the review began at eight, and I had no money for a cab. Each car that passed threw a fan of water onto the curb. I moved back, then forward again, unable to settle. My phone buzzed with a reminder from the school office: bring your portfolio. I read it twice, then stared at the empty road until my eyes stung. A woman under a broad umbrella offered to share it. I said I was fine, but my voice cracked on the last word. When the bus headlights appeared, I clutched the folder to my chest and waved with my free hand, nearly stepping into the street.

The rain soaked the cuffs of Gabriel’s trousers while he waited with a paper cup of coffee gone cold. He had promised his son he would be at the courthouse before the custody hearing began. His car had stalled two blocks away, and the tow truck dispatcher had put him on hold twice. Now the bus was seven minutes late. Gabriel called his lawyer and listened to it ring, gripping the phone so hard his knuckles blanched. A woman nearby shifted her shopping bags to make room on the bench. He thanked her but stayed standing, eyes fixed on the road. A bus swept past in the opposite direction, spraying muddy water over the curb. Gabriel flinched, then hurried to the route map and traced the line with a shaking finger. The next bus was the one he needed. He began pacing, checking the time after every few steps.

I left my passport on the kitchen table. The thought landed just as the bus pulled away from the stop, and I stood beneath the shelter roof watching its red taillights dissolve in the rain. My flight boarded at ten, and the passport was the one thing I couldn’t replace at the airport. I called my roommate, but her phone went straight to voicemail. The next bus was twenty minutes away. I ran to the corner, hoping to catch the driver at the traffic light, then slipped on the slick pavement and scraped my palm. A man waiting beside me handed over a tissue. I pressed it to my hand and tried to breathe slowly, but my chest kept hitching. When the bus arrived, I asked the driver if it stopped near my apartment. He nodded. I climbed aboard, dripping onto the steps, and held the rail with my uninjured hand.

At the stop outside the industrial park, Lena watched rainwater stream down the timetable. She had missed two shifts already while caring for her father, and the supervisor’s last message said another absence would end her contract. His breathing had worsened overnight; she had left him with a neighbor and promised to return before lunch. The bus was nowhere in sight. Lena called the neighbor, asked her to check the bedroom, then called again when there was no answer. Her lips moved silently as she counted minutes. A delivery driver offered her a lift, but the van was headed the wrong way. She thanked him, then turned toward the road again, twisting the strap of her work bag. When the bus finally arrived, she climbed aboard and asked the driver to go as fast as he could. He only pointed to the wet, crowded road ahead.

The rain had soaked the notice in my hand until the ink ran, but I could still read the words: final warning. My landlord wanted the rent by noon. I’d sold my guitar the night before and was carrying the cash in a folded envelope, checking the pocket every few seconds to make sure it was still there. The bus stop stood beside a closed laundromat; water dripped from its awning onto my neck. I tried calling the housing office, but the line kept disconnecting. Then I called my cousin and said I might need the spare room. I couldn’t make myself say the rest. When headlights appeared, I stepped forward and lifted the envelope like a ticket, though the driver couldn’t possibly see it. The bus pulled in. I climbed aboard, sat near the front, and held the cash between both hands.

At the rainy bus stop, Tomas read the text from his daughter’s school again: She has a fever. Please collect her. The message was forty minutes old. His bicycle chain had snapped on the way to work, and the bus was delayed behind traffic. He paced beneath the shelter, tapping the screen to refresh the route tracker. Nothing changed. His supervisor called; Tomas let it ring, then sent a message explaining that he had to leave. A gust drove rain sideways under the roof, speckling his glasses. He wiped them on his shirt and peered down the road. When a bus arrived, it was crowded, and the driver said the next stop was the end of the line. Tomas looked at the time, swallowed, and climbed aboard anyway. He stood in the aisle, one hand on the rail, silently working out how to get the rest of the way.

I kept the little envelope beneath my coat, away from the rain. It held the last of my savings, and I needed to reach the pharmacy before it closed to pick up medicine for my partner. The bus should have come at 6:15. At 6:32, I called the pharmacy and asked them to hold the prescription. The clerk said she could give me ten more minutes. I thanked her, then watched every car as if one might turn into the bus. My shoes made a wet sucking sound whenever I shifted my weight. A teenager beside me listened to music and hummed softly; I wanted to ask if he knew another route, but my throat felt tight. At last, the bus appeared, crawling through traffic. I waved both arms. It stopped, and I climbed on without waiting for the doors to open fully.

Nadia stood at the bus stop with a wet newspaper folded around a bouquet. She was meant to meet her sister at the ferry terminal before the morning crossing, carrying flowers for their father’s memorial. The bus had not arrived, and the clock above the bakery showed the crossing time approaching. Nadia called her sister, then listened to the message she had left earlier: I’m on my way. The words sounded far too calm. She walked to the corner to see if the bus was coming, hurried back, and checked the route number again. Rain dotted the petals, turning their pale edges translucent. A taxi passed with its sign lit but ignored her wave. She tucked the bouquet beneath her coat and asked a cyclist if the road ahead was blocked. He pointed toward an accident at the intersection. Nadia looked up the empty street and pressed the flowers close against her ribs.

Rain stitched silver lines across the shelter roof while I waited for the number 8. I set my canvas bag between my shoes and watched water gather in the cracks of the pavement. A sparrow hopped beneath the bench, inspected a crumb, and carried it off. My sleeve was damp at the cuff, but the chill felt easy to ignore. When a cyclist splashed through a puddle, I simply lifted my trousers above my ankles and let the spray pass. The bus was late, according to the sign. I checked my watch, then tucked it away; there was no useful answer hidden in its small hands. An older man arrived with a folded newspaper. I shifted over to make room, and we listened together to the rain tapping out its patient pattern.

At the stop outside the bakery, Amara balanced a paper cup beneath the edge of her umbrella and watched the morning traffic slide past. She was on her way to her first shift at the museum, but the bus had not appeared on schedule. Instead of pacing, she counted the lit windows above the shops and tried to guess which rooms held kitchens. A gust turned her umbrella inside out. She righted it with a small laugh, shook the drops from its ribs, and stood beneath the shelter beside a woman carrying tulips. They exchanged a nod. When the bus finally came, Amara let two passengers board ahead of her, then stepped up and wiped her shoes on the mat. The museum could wait another minute; the rain had already supplied the morning with something worth noticing.

I stood at the lakeside stop with my hood drawn close and my hands wrapped around a thermos. Rain blurred the far shore until the trees seemed to float. A delivery van rolled through the intersection, its tires making a soft hiss, and then the street returned to its steady drizzle. I had left home early for a dental appointment, so there was no need to watch every passing car. A child nearby was trying to keep a paper boat afloat in the gutter. When it snagged on a leaf, I crouched and nudged it free with the end of my umbrella. The child grinned, and I returned to the bench. My tea was still warm. I took one slow sip as the bus rounded the corner, its headlights shining through the watery air.

Leon, a retired electrician, waited beneath the narrow awning at the corner of Bell and Fourth. The rain had soaked the brim of his cap, so he removed it and rubbed the fabric between his fingers. He did not mind the delay. Across the road, a florist was arranging buckets of yellow daisies outside her shop, and Leon watched her work with the attention he once gave a complicated circuit. When the wind pushed rain under the awning, he stepped back without complaint. A young passenger asked whether the bus usually came this way. Leon pointed to the route map and explained the stops in an unhurried voice. Together they spotted the bus approaching through the mist. He slipped his cap on, tucked his hands into his coat, and waited for the doors to open.

The bus stop stood beside a row of maples, and rain shook loose their last copper leaves. I leaned my bicycle against the bench and sat with my helmet in my lap. The chain had slipped on the hill, but I had fixed it before deciding to take the bus the rest of the way. Grease marked one thumb. I rubbed it with a tissue, then watched the dark stain spread across the paper. A woman with a violin case arrived, carefully shielding its corners from the weather. We shared the dry end of the shelter without speaking. The route display flickered, went blank, then came back with the same arrival time. I smiled at the stubborn little screen. When the bus appeared, I stood, gave the violinist room to board first, and lifted my bicycle onto the rack.

Nadia waited at the stop outside the community garden, holding a bundle of leeks under her coat. Drops clung to the greenhouse panes, and the rows inside looked like neat green strokes on glass. She was returning from an early visit to her allotment, where the rain had saved her from carrying watering cans. A man hurried toward the shelter with his collar over his head. Nadia shifted her basket to make space and offered him a spare plastic bag for his damp gloves. He thanked her, and they watched the puddles gather along the curb. The bus was several minutes behind, yet she made no repeated checks of the timetable. She hummed a tune from the radio, quietly enough that only she could hear it. When the doors opened, she tucked the leeks more securely beneath her arm.

I waited outside the old cinema, where the bus shelter had a poster for a film I had already seen. Rain dotted the poster’s glass and turned the actor’s painted coat into a field of tiny lights. My appointment across town was not until nine, so I had brought a crossword in my pocket. I filled in three clues while water drummed above me, then paused to watch a dog nose along the curb. Its owner apologized for the muddy paw prints on the pavement. I told him the dog seemed to have found an important message. He laughed, and the animal wagged its tail. My shoes were wet around the edges, but my socks stayed dry. The bus arrived with a sigh of brakes. I folded the crossword along its crease and climbed aboard.

At dawn, Tomas waited for the bus beside the harbor, his lunch tin tucked under one arm. The rain darkened the wooden pier and peppered the water with dimples. He had worked the night shift at the fish market, and the ride home gave him time to let the clatter of scales and crates fade from his ears. A gull landed on the shelter roof, shook its wings, and stared down at him. Tomas opened his tin to check that his sandwich was still there, then closed it again. A woman carrying a violin case stepped under the shelter, and he moved his boots aside so she could stand out of the draft. They watched a fishing boat ease between the docks. When the bus came, Tomas climbed aboard and chose a seat by the window.

The rain began before I reached the stop, but my book was safe inside a waxed bag. I stood beneath the shelter with one shoulder against its painted post and turned to the page where I had left off. A few drops landed on the margin, so I brushed them away with my sleeve. The bus was late, and a notice on the pole blamed traffic downtown. I read the notice twice, then returned to the story instead of trying to guess how many minutes the delay would add. Beside me, a woman folded a damp newspaper into a neat square. We exchanged a brief smile when a gust sent a leaf skittering between our shoes. By the time headlights showed at the far end of the road, I had finished the chapter. I tucked in my bookmark and closed the cover.

Mina, who repaired watches in a shop near the station, waited beneath the bus shelter with a small toolbox at her feet. Rain threaded down the glass beside her, and she watched the drops race one another toward the metal frame. Her first customer would not arrive for another hour, so a delayed bus would not upset the day. She checked the toolbox latch, then used a handkerchief to dry the handle. A schoolboy nearby worried aloud that he had missed his stop. Mina showed him the route map and traced the line with one finger, explaining where he could transfer. Her voice stayed gentle, and he stopped twisting the strap of his backpack. When the bus pulled in, she helped him step around a broad puddle before lifting her own box aboard. The rain kept ticking on the roof.

I arrived at the stop carrying a paper bag of peaches for my sister. The rain had softened the bag at its corners, so I held it close against my coat and checked that the fruit had not shifted. A bus rolled by in the opposite direction, empty except for the driver, who raised a hand in greeting. I returned the wave and watched its red lights shrink around the bend. There was a bench beneath the shelter, but it was wet, so I stood and counted the drops sliding from the edge of the roof. A little girl asked whether the clouds would follow us all day. I said they might, but the peaches would still taste like summer. She considered this, then smiled. When our bus arrived, I climbed aboard carefully, keeping the bag level.

On a rainy morning in Northfield, Jasper waited for the bus outside the public library with a rolled-up watercolor tucked under his coat. The paper was protected by a cardboard tube, but he kept checking its cap whenever wind drove water beneath the shelter. Across the street, a baker carried trays through a back door, leaving the smell of warm bread in the wet air. Jasper breathed it in and adjusted the tube beneath his arm. His train of thought wandered to the painting he planned to finish: a row of houses reflected upside down in a puddle. A commuter asked him what he was carrying, and Jasper described the unfinished scene without rushing. Soon the bus appeared, tires brushing through shallow water. He secured the tube between his knees on board and watched the town slide by in silver streaks.

Rain stitched silver lines across the road while I stood beneath the bus-stop sign, holding my grocery bag away from a puddle. The schedule said 7:18. My phone said 7:31, and the route app kept spinning its little wheel as if that were useful information. I tapped the screen twice, then pressed the power button hard enough to make my thumb ache. A driver in a passing car sent a sheet of water over my shoes. I watched the bus lane, jaw tight, and checked the clock again. When the bus finally appeared, it rolled past with a cardboard OUT OF SERVICE notice in the front window. I let out a breath through my nose and lifted my free hand, though the driver was already gone. The next arrival estimate blinked from four minutes to twenty-two.

Marisol balanced her cello case between her knees and kept the rain from creeping beneath the shelter with the toe of her boot. She had left home early for the conservatory audition, but the bus had not shown, and the case’s damp latch refused to close. Each time headlights swelled at the corner, she straightened; each time a car swept by, her shoulders dropped a fraction. A man beside her studied the timetable and announced that the route was running normally. Marisol gave him a thin smile and pointed to the empty road. When the bus arrived, it stopped beyond the shelter, forcing her to drag the case through a gutter. The doors shut just as she reached them. She knocked once against the glass, then stood motionless, rain ticking on the case while the bus pulled away.

I had dressed for a sunny forecast, which now seemed like a personal joke. At the stop, rain soaked the cuffs of my trousers while I tried to fold a paper map small enough to fit in my pocket. The bus was supposed to take me to the courthouse before my name was called for jury duty. A teenager under the shelter kept bouncing a wet umbrella against my elbow. I shifted away, and he shifted too, without noticing. When the bus tracker announced that the vehicle had passed my stop, I stared at the screen until it refreshed. Nothing changed. I called the transit number and listened to music made from tinny piano notes. At last I ended the call, flattened the soggy map against the timetable, and muttered the route’s number under my breath.

Devon had promised his daughter he would be in the front row for her school play, and the rain was already blurring the ink on his ticket. He waited at the stop with a toolbox tucked beneath one arm, watching buses from other routes glide past. The electronic sign displayed ARRIVING, then changed to DELAYED without explanation. He jabbed the button for the pedestrian crossing, though the light had no bearing on the bus. A woman offered to share her umbrella; Devon thanked her, then paced to the curb and back, counting each turn. When a city bus finally came, the driver lowered a window and explained that it was full. Devon looked at the empty space beside the driver, pressed his lips together, and stepped back beneath the shelter. He phoned the school and asked them to save a seat.

My coffee lid popped loose just as I reached the bus stop, and warm coffee ran down my hand into the rainwater on the pavement. I set the cup on the bench and wiped my fingers with a receipt, getting ink across my palm. The morning had started with a broken printer at work; now the bus was eleven minutes late, according to the sign that had been saying eleven minutes for what felt like half an hour. I pressed the stop button on the pole, then remembered the bus wasn’t there yet. A cyclist splashed through the gutter, and I moved my laptop bag behind my legs. When the bus appeared, it slowed, then continued past without opening its doors. I picked up the coffee, looked at the lid, and crushed it flat in my fist.

Nadia stood at the stop with a bouquet wrapped in brown paper, trying to keep the flowers upright beneath her coat. She was on her way to visit her mother in the hospital, and the rain had turned the paper soft around the stems. The bus should have arrived ten minutes earlier. A digital display flashed a cheerful sun icon beside the word RAIN, and Nadia stared at it as if waiting for it to correct itself. She shifted the bouquet from one arm to the other, then shook water from her sleeve with a sharp flick. When a bus finally pulled in, the driver announced that it would terminate two stops short because of roadworks. Nadia closed her eyes for a moment, tightened the damp ribbon, and asked which connection would still get her there.

I stood under the narrow awning with my work boots planted on the only dry patch of concrete. The rain blew sideways, so the patch kept shrinking. My supervisor had already texted that the loading dock could not wait, and the bus tracker’s tiny icon had been frozen halfway along the route for ages. I refreshed it until my screen went dark, then wiped the glass on my sleeve and tried again. A woman beside me said the buses were always late in this weather. I gave a short laugh that came out more like a cough. When the bus arrived, its front tire hit a pothole and sprayed the shelter. I pulled my collar over my mouth, climbed aboard, and found the fare machine displaying PLEASE TRY AGAIN. Behind me, the line began to grow.

At sixty-eight, Ernest had learned to leave extra time for everything, but this morning’s rain had defeated even his careful schedule. He waited for the bus with a paper bag of warm rolls held against his chest. Water gathered along the brim of his hat and dripped onto his glasses. He cleaned them with a handkerchief, only to fog them again with his breath. The timetable had been replaced by a blank plastic frame, and nobody nearby knew whether the route had changed. Ernest tapped his walking stick against the curb in a steady rhythm. When a bus finally stopped, the ramp failed to lower. The driver tried the controls again while passengers watched. Ernest turned his face toward the rain, then asked if there was another vehicle coming, his voice clipped and careful.

I was carrying a tray of cupcakes to the bakery where I worked, with one hand beneath the cardboard and the other gripping my umbrella. The wind turned the umbrella inside out before I even reached the bus stop. I wrestled it closed, and one cupcake slid into the side of its box. The route board promised a bus every ten minutes, but the last one had passed twenty minutes ago. I called the bakery to say I might be late and listened to my manager sigh through the phone. A drop landed right on the frosting of the cupcake nearest the lid. I stared at it, set the tray carefully on the bench, and tried to repair the icing with a plastic knife from my pocket. When headlights appeared, I snatched up the box and waved both arms.

Sanjay was heading to an immigration appointment with a folder tucked beneath his jacket. The rain made the papers curl at the edges, and he kept checking that the important form was still there. At the bus stop, a printed notice said the route had been diverted, but the map beneath it showed no alternate path. He read the notice again, slower this time, then folded it back into place with a sharp crease. A delivery van blocked the curb, leaving buses unable to pull in close. When one finally arrived, it stopped in the traffic lane and the driver opened the doors only after several cars honked. Sanjay climbed aboard sideways, protecting the folder with his shoulder. He asked whether the bus still reached the office and received a shrug from the driver.

I had promised myself I would arrive at the job interview calm, prepared, and dry. At the bus stop, my résumé was tucked inside a plastic sleeve, but rain had soaked through the seam and softened the pages. I pressed them between my palms, trying to straighten the corners. The arrival screen switched from six minutes to nine, then back to six, as though it were playing a game. I paced from the bench to the sign and back, counting the cracks in the pavement. A man asked if I knew when the bus was coming. I pointed at the screen and said, “Apparently, it’s deciding.” My voice sounded sharper than I meant. When the bus finally rounded the corner, I shoved the damp résumé into my bag and wiped my hands on my coat.

Lila waited at the stop with a sleeping toddler in a carrier and a sack of laundry balanced against her hip. The rain drummed on the shelter roof, loud enough to cover the traffic, but not the baby’s occasional whimper. She had planned the trip around the laundromat’s last open machines, and every minute mattered. The bus was late, then the sign went blank. Lila rocked from heel to toe, careful not to jostle the child, and used one finger to clear water from the screen of her phone. A bus swept through the intersection without stopping, its windows fogged and crowded. She watched it disappear, then looked down at the laundry bag, which had begun to sag in the wet. When the next bus came, she stepped forward and asked the driver to lower the ramp.
